lessons.title: Fretboard map 1
lessons.focus: Natural notes on low E and A
learningObjectives: Explain or demonstrate the main idea: natural notes on low e and a.
Perform the target task accurately at a comfortable, controlled tempo.
Apply the skill in a short musical context and identify one next improvement.

explanation.keyIdea: The fretboard is a repeating pitch map. Each adjacent fret is one semitone; after the note sequence A–G, the letter names repeat in the next octave. Octave shapes connect the same note name in different places.
explanation.plainLanguage: This lesson focuses on natural notes on low e and a. Treat the written checkpoint as an observable target, not a deadline. First understand the sound or movement, then practise a small part, then return to the musical whole.
explanation.workedExample: Low E/A note map, 2 minutes daily

demonstrationOrReference.referenceSuggestion: Use a clear, slow demonstration of natural notes on low e and a from a reputable guitar-learning source or your own view of the fretboard. Compare the demonstration with the step-by-step guide here; no paid-course video or protected tab is reproduced.
steps: Start from a known open-string note and move one fret at a time, naming each semitone.
Use the natural-note sequence A, B, C, D, E, F, G; remember B–C and E–F are adjacent semitones.
Find the same note on another string using an octave shape, then verify it by sound or a tuner/reference pitch.

lessonBlocks.content: Before playing, listen to the target sound, sing or count it where possible, and identify what you want to notice.

lessons.title: CAGED and advanced fretboard map

learningObjectives: Explain or demonstrate the main idea: connect open shapes, movable regions and octave landmarks.
Perform the target task accurately at a comfortable, controlled tempo.
Apply the skill in a short musical context and identify one next improvement.

explanation.keyIdea: A chord is a set of notes heard together. A shape is only one way to arrange those notes: identify the root and chord quality, form the shape efficiently, then check the individual strings before adding rhythm.
explanation.plainLanguage: This lesson focuses on connect open shapes, movable regions and octave landmarks. Treat the written checkpoint as an observable target, not a deadline. First understand the sound or movement, then practise a small part, then return to the musical whole.
explanation.workedExample: CAGED map with root notes and octave links across two positions

demonstrationOrReference.referenceSuggestion: Use a clear, slow demonstration of connect open shapes, movable regions and octave landmarks from a reputable guitar-learning source or your own view of the fretboard. steps: Name the chord and identify its root; use a chord diagram or the stated string/fret pattern as a map.
Place fingers close to the fret wires, one at a time, and keep unused strings intentionally open or muted.
Pick each intended string separately, correct muted or buzzing notes, then strum a slow pulse.

lessonBlocks.content: Ear learning follows a repeatable loop: listen, sing or hum, identify the contour or rhythm, find a possible note on the instrument, then verify by listening again. Singing is a practical bridge between hearing and playing.

lessonBlocks.title: See and try it slowly
content: Set up the instrument comfortably, tune if needed, and check that the exercise is pain-free.
Listen to a short phrase several times without touching the guitar.
Hum the rhythm and contour; note whether it rises, falls or repeats.
Find the first note, then work through the phrase one small interval at a time and compare your attempt with the reference.
Work on this week's target: Three-piece set: acoustic, rhythm-guitar and lead/blues excerpts. Begin below the suggested reference tempo of 72 BPM if accuracy is not yet secure.
Apply the skill in a musical phrase or progression; keep the pulse going through a small error.
Finish by recalling the key idea without looking and recording one observation.
